blocks.text: Carole Bellaïche: What the image is still searching for

With À ta recherche ( In Search of You ), Carole Bellaïche continues an artistic practice that never merely photographs reality, but questions what lingers within it. For her, the image is not a way of stopping time, but an unstable surface where the present, memory and absence overlap. To photograph is less about preserving than about placing what remains in tension with what has disappeared. The title of the book immediately introduces this ambiguity. À ta recherche implies a research, but also an impossibility: that of ever fully finding what one is looking for. Photography thus becomes the very space of this quest, with all the displacement, projection and gaps it entails. This approach finds a particularly fertile counterpoint in Yannick Haenel’s text. Literature does not explain the images, any more than the photographs illustrate the text: together, they construct a mental territory in which the visible is constantly traversed by what escapes it.

In À ta recherche , Carole Bellaïche thus shifts documentary photography towards a more elusive territory, where the image becomes both an experience of memory and an instrument of thought. What matters is no longer simply what the photograph shows, but what it brings back afterwards: a sensation, an absence, an incomplete story, sometimes even an image we thought we had forgotten. It is in this space between – between appearance and disappearance, presence and absence, reality and memory -that the strength of her work lies today.

“A ta recherche” by Carole Bellaiche and Yannick Haenel, édition Gallimard
The beginning of a series sometimes comes from a particular encounter. What was the starting point for À ta recherche ?

Carole Bellaïche: I started this series five years ago, photographing this young couple, with whom I immediately felt a real connection, in the Bois de Vincennes. They were both very comfortable in front of the camera, so I had fun creating very theatrical double-exposure images, inspired by the book Spoon River by the Italian master Mario Giacomelli. I very quickly discovered in the young woman a naturalness that I had hardly ever photographed before, and it made me want to continue this adventure.
To photograph intimacy: is it about crossing a boundary or abolishing a distance?

Carole Bellaïche: It is undoubtedly about crossing a barrier. It means getting closer, looking, provoking something in my subjects. There is something voyeuristic and provocative about it as well. I also try to convey messages through my images. Images of love are beautiful, poetic images that make you dream, and that is what I want to translate. And despite the few staged elements, the intimacy is real because they are a real couple.
You say that you want to translate love into images. What can photography capture that words cannot hold on to?

Carole Bellaïche: Everything! My language is really photography. That is how I have always expressed myself. The immediacy of an image triggers emotions and sensations that are much easier to capture than with words. Obviously, for me, it is easier to make images than to write. With actresses, for example, my relationship with them is photographic. It is my language.
The book then brings literature into your photographic language. How did your encounter with Yannick Haenel come about?

Carole Bellaïche: As I said earlier, I made the images for this book inspired by Giacomelli, and I was advised to meet Yannick. It was a bit of a gamble because all the photographs had already been made. When we met in a café and I spread my images out in front of him, he immediately said to me: “I want to write a story about your photographs.” I wanted a fictional, novelistic text. He had carte blanche and made the work his own, while keeping certain fragments that were important to me, such as Tunisia, which is the country my parents come from. It gave me a way of going there, following in the footsteps of a youth I knew nothing about, as well as the extraordinary garden that once belonged to Leila Menchari. Eight months later, I received his text, which I obviously found very moving.
Is the woman you photograph, in some way, a self-portrait?

Carole Bellaïche: No, not at all. I have always photographed women who are the opposite of me. I have always had this fantasy of the blonde woman with light eyes. My mother was a redhead with green eyes, so perhaps that had some influence, it is possible… But I must also admit that what interests me more than self-portraiture is looking at the other.
You photograph faces extensively. What do you look for first in a gaze?

Carole Bellaïche: The most important thing for me is the intensity of the gaze. It is really what makes me want to photograph someone. There is something that passes through a gaze, something that can be very difficult to explain. I may be drawn to a face, but it is often the gaze that triggers the image. The artistic or aesthetic aspect, if you prefer, comes afterwards, with a certain harmony that allows me to explore its beauty. But beauty alone does not really interest me. What interests me is what lies behind it, what the face allows you to see. I like it when a photograph makes you want to keep looking, because you feel that there is something you cannot completely understand.
Do your images speak more of a presence, or of the possibility of an absence?

Carole Bellaïche: Instinctively, I would say: a presence. Even in the absence of certain places, there are traces of a presence. A photograph can show someone who is no longer there, but for me, what remains in the image is precisely that presence. A light, an object, a place, an attitude can be enough to make someone felt. I am not necessarily trying to photograph absence, but rather what remains of it, what continues to live in our memory. Perhaps that is also why certain images take on a different meaning over time. They become traces of something we have experienced, or something we have loved.
At what point does a photograph cease to be a memory and become fiction?

Carole Bellaïche: I think photography is always, to some extent, fiction. Even when it is very realistic, there is inevitably a choice, a framing, a light, a way of looking. For me, staging does not take anything away from the truth of an image. On the contrary, it can sometimes reveal something more intimate, something deeper. In this book, the characters really exist, their story really exists, but the images also tell something that may never actually have happened. That is where fiction becomes interesting.
After so many portraits, what remains elusive in a face?

Carole Bellaïche: Everything that cannot be seen. You can photograph a face, a gaze, an expression, but you never really know what is going on behind it. That is precisely what interests me. I can have the feeling that I know someone through a photograph and, at the same time, know that something is still escaping me. That is probably why I continue to photograph other people: to try to understand, even though I know I will never have the complete answer.
An exhibition is, I believe, set to follow the publication of the book. Could you tell us a little about it?

Carole Bellaïche: With pleasure. It will be a short exhibition. It opens on November 19th at Signature, Rue Jean-Pierre Thimbaud, with around forty black-and-white gelatin silver prints. There will be mainly still lifes.
Text and Interview by Carole Schmitz
